skill-create-skill.title: kes-create-skill: create, edit and review skills the right way
skill-create-skill.note: It controls the process, not the exact result · An interview that avoids parroting and guides you all the way through · A 20-question test set and a cold review by a helper.

sections.t: AI finishes the job, then next time you have to explain everything again?
sections.lead: AI is like a skilled intern who has no process handbook, so it does the job a different way every time. Instead of repeating your instructions every day, you can package your method into a standard skill.
ticks: It controls the process, not the exact result
An interview that avoids parroting and guides you all the way through
A 20-question test set and a cold review by a helper

sections.t: Make AI follow one process, instead of working on a whim

items.t: It controls the process, not the exact result
items.d: A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file that the AI reads and follows step by step, the way you set it up. A skill does not force the AI to produce the same result. It makes the AI follow the same process every time it runs.

items.t: An interview that avoids parroting and guides you all the way through
items.d: kes-create-skill asks you in groups of 2-5 questions with suggestions, so you only need to nod or pick quickly. The process has 5 required questions, so the skill works for many similar cases and not just the one you just did.

items.t: A 20-question test set and a cold review by a helper
items.d: The AI drafts 20 test prompts (10 where the skill must trigger, 10 similar ones where it must stay quiet) for you to approve before scoring. Each side must get at least 9/10 right. A helper that knows nothing about your conversation does a "cold" review, and each issue points to a file and line. If the AI cannot open a helper, it reviews the skill itself and says clearly that it was a self-review.

Edit gives you a backup kept outside the skill folder, plus a list of what changed and what was deliberately NOT changed. Score only reports issues and does not fix them. Optimize gives you a before/after report and a checklist showing whether each old point was kept or cut, with a reason.

sections.t: Turn hands-on experience into an asset you can reuse

items.t: A shop owner who needs to send customers a standard quote every day
items.before: Every time, you copy and paste the price list, tell the AI to keep the template, and ask it to calculate carefully.
items.after: Just say 'Create a skill for me from what I just did: draft a quote using the shop's template'. Next time, one sentence and it's done.

items.t: A content creator who is writing posts and managing what gets published
items.before: The caption-writing skill works for a while, then starts skipping the step that checks product prices.
items.after: Say "Edit my caption-writing skill": the AI reads the whole original, makes a backup, edits, tests, then bumps the version number, with a list of what changed and what was deliberately not changed.

items.t: A busy person who needs a weekly market shopping menu that suits the family's tastes
items.before: Every week you retype the list of dishes and each person's foods to avoid, and tell the AI to sort items by market stall.
items.after: Package your family's routine as a skill. At the start of the week, one sentence and the AI follows those steps, with no need to repeat each person's foods to avoid.

items.t: A team lead who is getting ready to hand over working documents to teammates
items.before: You wrote a skill yourself but are not sure whether the wording is padded or whether it misses any technical step.
items.after: Say "Review this skill for me, don't change anything" to get a report in a fixed format, with each issue pointing to a file and line, before you pass it to teammates.

items.t: A user who already has a skill but sees the AI skipping steps or triggering it by mistake
items.before: A skill that drags on makes the AI skip steps, or it triggers even when you ask about something else.
items.after: Use the optimize branch to trim extra words, adjust the description, and check it with the 20-question test set.

sections.t: How to use it

items.d: Download the zip file, give it to the AI and say: 'Install the skill in this file following the INSTALL.md inside.'
Open a new conversation and say: 'Create a skill for me from what I just did: ...' (or choose edit, review or optimize).
Answer the interview briefly, approve the brief and the test prompts, and you get a complete skill folder with a zip file.

sections.t: Frequently asked questions

items.q: What language is the skill written in?
items.a: The body of the skill is written in short English, so the AI reads and follows it more reliably. The prompts that call the skill and anything your customers see stay in Vietnamese, and the report sent to you is in your own language.

items.q: Does this skill run the work for me or build automated workflows?
items.a: No. This skill does not run installed skills for you, does not write process documents for people to read, and does not build automated flows inside workflow tools.

items.q: Can I use it to edit a skill released by a tool vendor?
items.a: We recommend not editing it directly, because the vendor's updates will overwrite your changes. Put your customizations in the project instruction file, or create a small companion skill.

items.q: What do I need to install on my computer?
items.a: Node.js, to measure the skill's length (free software; without it, the AI counts by hand and says clearly that it is a hand count). By default, the AI scores by hand against the 20-question set. The automated test round is optional, runs only on some command-line AI tools, calls the AI several hundred times so it uses up your AI plan's quota, and the AI will ask before running it.

items.q: Who is listed as the author of the finished skill?
items.a: The default author is your name, along with the line 'built with kes-create-skill · KesFlow'. If you want to remove this line, just tell the AI in one sentence while creating the skill.

items.q: Does a skill guarantee the AI always produces the same result?
items.a: No. A skill makes the AI follow the same process every time, not produce the same result, and we do not promise the skill triggers correctly 100% of the time. The quality of the skill depends on your answers during the interview. If something is unclear, just say "I don't know yet".

items.q: What if my AI cannot create files on my computer?
items.a: The AI gives you each file right in the chat and says clearly where that file belongs.

sections.t: Package your method into a skill
sections.d: Download the zip file, give it to your AI and send one message, and the AI installs it itself. Then open a new conversation and say "create a skill for me from what I just did".
sections.note: The included README also has a roughly 15-minute read on how to think about writing skills, so you understand the idea behind them instead of just using the tool.

guide-ai-agent-theory.title: What is an AI Agent? What it really is and how it differs from an AI chatbot
guide-ai-agent-theory.note: Understand what an agent really is, how it differs from ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini in Q&A mode, and what parts it's made of.

next.label: Read next: The AI Agent ecosystem (OpenClaw, Hermes, MCP…)

sections.t: A chatbot answers questions. An agent takes a goal and gets it done.
sections.lead: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini used in a Q&A chat window are chatbots. The same model, given tools, memory and permission to act, can work as an agent. This card explains what an agent really is, its 6 parts, the levels of autonomy and the risks to know.
ticks: The 6-step loop of an agent
A chatbot vs agent comparison table
Risks and golden rules before you delegate

sections.t: One line to remember: a chatbot answers questions. An agent takes a goal, breaks it into steps, uses tools to do the work and reports back.
After reading, you will

items.d: A system that uses an LLM as its brain, with tools, memory, workflows and permissions, running in a loop until the job is done or stopping to ask you.

items.t: Tell a chatbot from an agent
items.d: A comparison by goal, how it runs, tools, memory, initiative, real-world impact and risk, plus three questions to spot an agent.

items.t: Know the 6 parts of an agent
items.d: Brain, tools, memory, skills, runtime environment and communication channel: each part has its own job.

items.t: Know how to grant permissions safely
items.d: Three levels of autonomy from fixed workflow to autonomous agent, plus risks like overly broad permissions, prompt injection and unexpected costs.

sections.t: What an AI Agent really is

An AI Agent is a system that uses a large language model (LLM) as its “brain”, surrounded by the things that let it act: tools, memory, workflows and permissions. Instead of stopping at one answer, an agent runs in a loop until the job is done, or stops to ask you when a decision is needed.

items.d: You hand over a job, no need to give every small command.
The agent breaks the job into steps.
Search the web, read files, call APIs, run commands, control apps.
Read back what the tools return and check it matches the intent.
Keep going or change direction until the goal is reached.
Send the results, check back at important or irreversible steps.

sections.t: How an AI chatbot and an AI Agent differ

ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini… used in a Q&A chat window are AI chatbots. The same model can act as an agent when given tools, memory and permission to act. So the difference lies in how the system is built around the model, not just in the model itself.

head: Criteria
AI chatbot (Q&A)
AI Agent
rows: Complete a multi-step task (read meeting notes, create tasks, schedule…)
One turn: you ask, it answers
A loop: plan, act, check, continue
Call APIs, browse the web, read/write files, run code, control apps
Lasting across days: notes, document stores, logs
Can run on a schedule or on events, then report to you
Takes real actions itself (sends email, writes records, edits files) within granted scope
Low: if it's wrong, you see it right away
Higher: mistakes can have real consequences; needs permissions and approval
You need to be good at
Delegating clearly, setting boundaries, checking results

sections.t: The line is blurring: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini all have agent modes (tools, web browsing, running code…). Ask yourself three questions: (1) Does it plan multiple steps on its own? (2) Does it use tools to act on the outside world? (3) Does it remember and keep running when you're not there? The more “yes” answers, the more it's an agent.
A quick comparison

items.d: You paste meeting notes into the chat and ask for a summary. It returns a summary; you create the tasks and schedule yourself.
You send the notes file. The agent reads it, pulls out the action items, creates tasks, puts them on the calendar, messages the people involved and reports back to you.

sections.t: The 6 parts of an AI Agent

items.d: The language model reads intent, breaks down the work, decides the next step.
APIs, browser, files, commands, apps. The MCP standard makes connecting tools easier.
Your context and data: notes, documents, history, so you don't have to explain again.
Workflows you've packaged as instructions so the agent redoes them the right way.
Software that holds the loop, permissions, schedules, cost limits and logs.
Where you hand over work and get results: Zalo, Telegram, Slack, email…

sections.t: Levels of autonomy

items.d: You design the steps up front; AI handles a few of them (summarizing, classifying). Easiest to control.
The agent plans and acts on its own; you approve the important steps.
Runs long, decides many steps on its own; you only see results and alerts. Needs tight permissions and monitoring.

sections.t: Beginners should start at levels 1 and 2, then widen permissions gradually as they come to trust the results.
Risks to know before letting an agent work

items: Permissions too broad: the more an agent can do, the more harm a mistake causes. Grant minimum permissions.
Malicious instructions hidden in content the agent reads (emails, web pages, files), also called prompt injection. Don't let the agent follow everything it reads.
Unexpected costs: loops that run forever or call the model too often. Set a budget limit.
Mistakes nobody notices: keep logs so you can review what the agent did.
Leaked keys and data: don't put real passwords or API keys where the agent or others can read them.

sections.t: Golden rules: minimum permissions, approve every irreversible action, set a cost cap, turn on logging, keep secret keys separate from the data the agent reads.
FAQ

items.q: Are ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini chatbots or agents?
items.a: Used in a Q&A chat window, they're chatbots. All three have agent modes (tools, web browsing, running code...). The difference lies in how the system is built around the model, not just in the model itself.

items.q: How can I tell whether a tool is an agent?
items.a: Ask three questions: does it plan multiple steps on its own, does it use tools to act on the outside world, does it remember and keep running when you're not there. The more “yes” answers, the more it's an agent.

items.q: How much autonomy should a beginner give an agent?
items.a: Start at level 1 (fixed workflow) and level 2 (agent with human approval), then widen permissions gradually as you come to trust the results.

items.q: What is prompt injection?
items.a: Malicious instructions hidden in content the agent reads, such as emails, web pages, files. Don't let the agent follow everything it reads.

items.q: How do I keep an agent from running up unexpected costs?
items.a: Set a budget limit to avoid loops that run forever or call the model too often, and turn on logging so you can review what the agent did.

sections.t: Delegate to an agent like you would to a new hire: a clear job, clear boundaries
sections.d: Start at levels 1 and 2 and widen permissions gradually as you trust the results. Read The AI Agent ecosystem next to meet the actual tools.
sections.note: Minimum permissions, approve every irreversible action, set a cost cap, turn on logging, keep secret keys separate from the data the agent reads.

skill-self-explorer.title: self-explorer: self-discovery from 3 angles
skill-self-explorer.note: The AI becomes the one who asks the questions · Real life always comes first · A clear 10-part portrait report.

sections.t: When your tests and your chart each say something different
sections.lead: You have taken the MBTI, looked at numerology or Tử Vi (Vietnamese astrology), and each source points a different way. After reading many readings, you still can't say who you really are or what you want to live for.
ticks: The AI becomes the one who asks the questions
Real life always comes first
A clear 10-part portrait report

sections.t: Bring 3 views together and ask directly about the contradictions

items.t: The AI becomes the one who asks the questions
items.d: The AI gathers your chart, any test results you already have, and your own written story (about 500-2000 words). Then it asks, one question at a time, exactly where they contradict each other. The follow-up and cross-checking part takes about 10-12 questions. If your answer is vague, the AI asks for one concrete example.

Every conclusion points back to a sentence you wrote or a test result. The chart is only a reference lens, kept in its own section. When the chart and real life disagree, the AI always puts your actual experience first.

The real person, a summary of the 3 views, where they match and where they still conflict, core strengths, wounds and blind spots, life values, the mission statement, aesthetics, what is draining your energy, and questions to reflect on. The report is a mirror, not a plan.

items.t: Direct, and respectful of your limits
items.d: If there isn't enough data, the report says plainly that the mission statement is unclear. It does not force out a sentence just to have one. If there is something you don't want to talk about, say so and the AI won't push. "I don't know" is not counted as dodging.

sections.t: A mirror for your career and life crossroads

items.t: A working person at a career crossroads, thinking about changing jobs or fields
items.before: Torn between what others expect and what they like, and unable to see where their real strengths lie.
items.after: You get a portrait that shows your core strengths and what drains your energy. Each point links back to a sentence you wrote yourself. It is a base for you to weigh your own direction.

items.t: Someone who has just been through a major event or is entering a new stage, such as graduating, quitting a job, or becoming a parent
items.before: Their routine is shaken, and the old definitions of themselves no longer fit their current reality.
items.after: A report that puts the different views side by side: what still fits, what has changed, and questions to reflect on at your own pace.

items.t: Someone with MBTI, DISC or chart results who doesn't see themselves in them in real life
items.before: Forcing their behavior into a theoretical mold even though their intuition says otherwise.
items.after: A clear split between where theory matches lived experience and where it conflicts, so you no longer feel forced into a label.

items.t: A small business owner or personal-brand builder who needs to distill core values
items.before: A pile of polished slogans that sound good but have no evidence from real stories.
items.after: Life values written out with evidence from your own story. If the data isn't enough, the report says clearly what is missing.

items.t: Anyone who wants to look back at themselves at the end of the year
items.before: The year passed in a blur, with no clear sense of what drives them or what is quietly wearing them down.
items.after: A report with its own sections for "what is draining your energy" and "questions to reflect on", based on what you told it.

sections.t: See it in action: input → process → output
Self-discovery while weighing a job change

input.label: You provide
input.t:
I want to explore myself, help me understand who I really am.
Attached: MBTI and DISC results I already have, birth date, time and place, a self-written story of about 1,200 words.

steps: Gathers your chart, the test results you already have, and your own story.
Asks one question at a time exactly where the sources contradict each other, about 10-12 questions; vague answers get a request for a concrete example.
Cross-checks, and when the chart and real life disagree, puts your real experience first.
Writes a 10-part portrait report, with every conclusion pointing back to something you wrote or a test result.

output.label: 10-part portrait report
output.t:
1. The real person: the one who untangles things for the team, needs time alone to recharge.
2. Summary of 3 views: tests, chart, your story.
3. Matches and conflicts: introversion matches; "likes to lead" (chart) doesn't match real life.
4. Core strengths: turning messy work into clear steps (evidence: when you rebuilt the stock process).
5. Wounds and blind spots: hard to say no, takes on extra work, then burns out.
6. Life values: control of your own time; finishing things properly.
7. Mission statement: not enough data to settle it, not forced just to have one.
8. Aesthetics: clean, few details, prefers quiet spaces.
9. What drains your energy: long meetings with no conclusion.
10. Question to reflect on: "Which work leaves you with energy to spare?"

sections.note: Illustrative example, real content depends on your story. Not psychotherapy, not fortune telling.

sections.t:
[T3 · Critical · open] Your test result leans introverted, but in your story there are three times you volunteered to organize the whole group. In those moments, did you feel energized or drained? Tell me about one specific time.

You: At the project launch event, I stepped in to coordinate because I was anxious about the work running late. When it was over I was exhausted and had to be alone for the whole weekend to recover.

AI: Noted for point T3 for now, and I'll keep cross-checking: your organizing ability comes from a sense of responsibility and a wish to control the schedule, not from a need to draw energy from a crowd. This fits the introverted side of your test, but it shows up in practice as taking the load on yourself.

Section 6: LIFE VALUES
- Autonomy: You value the right to decide your own work rhythm more than a big title.
Evidence: your story about turning down a manager role in 2023 to keep control of your time.
- Full responsibility: You only feel at ease when work is done to the standard you set for yourself.
Evidence: your story about staying up all night to fix a system failure even though no one assigned it to you.

Section 7: MISSION STATEMENT
- Status: Not enough data to settle it.
- Note: Your writing focuses mostly on past events. It doesn't yet show the long-term impact you want to have on the people around you. We won't force out a sentence just to have one. If you want, tell us more about what you hope to leave for others, then continue.
sections.cap: Report excerpt: life values with evidence, mission left unforced (fictional example)

sections.t: How to use it

items.d: Give the zip file to the AI and say: 'Install the skill in this file following the INSTALL.md inside.'
Open a new conversation and say: 'I want to explore myself. Help me understand who I really am.'
Send your information and any test results you have, write your own story, and answer the cross-check questions. You can pause midway. Just keep the path to the notes file so you can continue.

sections.t: Frequently asked questions

items.q: Is this skill psychological therapy?
items.a: No. The skill does not diagnose or give medical, legal or financial advice. If it sees you are in crisis, the AI will stop and suggest you see a mental health professional.

items.q: Does the skill predict the future or tell fortunes?
items.a: No. The chart is only a reference lens in its own section. It is not used to predict luck or the future. The report is a mirror of the present, not a plan or a verdict.

items.q: Do I take an MBTI or DISC test during the session?
items.a: No. You bring results you already have. If you have none, skip them, and the AI won't make you take a test. The report then relies on your own story and your chart, and says clearly what is missing.

items.q: Does the report come with an action plan or a career-change roadmap?
items.a: Not on its own. The report is a mirror, not a plan. If you want a 30-day plan or a 6-month roadmap, ask the AI after you read the report.

items.q: Where do my data and stories go?
items.a: Apart from the AI service you are chatting with, the skill sends your data nowhere else, unless you agree to look up your chart on the web (it only sends date, time, place of birth and gender, not your name). Deleting the 2 notes files and the report deletes the skill's saved copies. The content stays in your AI tool's chat history until you delete it. If your AI app has a memory feature, turn it off before the session if you don't want it to remember.

items.q: Can I still use the skill if I don't remember my birth time?
items.a: Yes. Knowing the rough hour (Tý hour, Sửu hour...) is enough for a Tử Vi chart. If you don't know the hour, the rising sign, the houses and the Tử Vi chart are left blank. The AI calculates numerology and the Sun sign itself.

sections.t: See yourself clearly with your AI teammate
sections.d: Download the zip file, give it to your AI and send one message, and the AI installs it itself. The session can run long, and you can pause midway.
sections.note: Not psychological therapy, and not a prediction of the future. The skill works best on a strong reasoning AI model.

skill-reflect.title: reflect: end-of-session retrospective
skill-reflect.note: A 5-part review that fits on one screen · Each lesson filed in the right place to be remembered · A strict 4-question filter, and nothing is saved until you approve.

sections.t: Don't let your AI staff lose their memory every morning
sections.lead: When a job is done, all the good lessons vanish with the chat window you just closed. Open a new session and the AI forgets everything, old mistakes come back, and you have to explain it all again from scratch.
ticks: A 5-part review that fits on one screen
Each lesson filed in the right place to be remembered
A strict 4-question filter, and nothing is saved until you approve

sections.t: A lessons-learned notebook that makes teamwork with AI smoother

items.t: A 5-part review that fits on one screen
items.d: The AI looks back at the conversation you just finished and settles 5 points: What happened, What went well, What didn't go well, Do better next time, and Proposed notes. It relies only on real work from the session, and it stays short and concrete.

items.t: Each lesson filed in the right place to be remembered
items.d: Instruction is for principles that apply to every job, Memory is for facts or preferences about you and your project, and Skill is for repeatable procedures, including the places where mistakes are easy to make. Something that happened only once is not saved anywhere, because the review already keeps it.

items.t: A strict 4-question filter, and nothing is saved until you approve
items.d: Every proposal must pass 4 questions: does it already exist (the AI opens the exact place it plans to write to and reads it), how many times has it happened, is it going in the right place, and is there a real case attached. A rejected proposal still shows up as one line with the reason. The AI saves only what you agree to.

items.t: Switch sessions without losing the thread, thanks to a handoff
items.d: Say "reflect and hand off" and you get an extra block to paste into the new conversation: the goal, where things stand, key files, next steps, and traps already hit. The AI reads the real state at that moment. Anything it can't check is marked "not checked".

sections.t: Turn every work session into hands-on experience for your AI

items.t: A tenant or landlord has just drafted a rental contract with the AI
items.before: The next time you draft a different contract, the AI forgets the special deposit terms, and you have to fix it all over again.
items.after: The AI looks back at the session and proposes adding a deposit-terms check step to the contract-drafting skill you already use (if you have no skill yet, it gives you the steps as text to paste in when you do this again).

items.t: An accountant or business owner has just finished this month's payroll
items.before: The AI got one allowance wrong. You fixed it in the conversation and that was it, so the same mistake comes back next month.
items.after: The review spells out what went wrong and proposes adding a check step to the payroll skill you already use. The AI saves it only if you approve.

items.t: A professional is in the middle of a long task and the conversation has grown too long, so a new one is needed
items.before: In a new conversation the AI knows nothing, and you have to retype the background, the documents and the unfinished items.
items.after: Say "reflect and hand off" and the AI gives you a note covering where the work stands, key files, next steps and traps already hit, so you can paste it into the new conversation and carry on.

items.t: A content creator has just had a session writing a fanpage post in exactly the voice they wanted
items.before: In the next session the AI writes in a generic voice again, and you have to repeat everything you adjusted last time.
items.after: The AI pulls out what worked this time and proposes saving it in the right place, so you don't have to repeat it next time.

items.t: An individual planning a trip or a family birthday party
items.before: Every time you ask about places to eat and visit, the AI suggests meat dishes and faraway venues, even though your family is vegetarian and prefers short trips.
items.after: The AI notices the repeated habit and proposes saving your family's vegetarian diet and travel limits to Memory.

sections.t: How to use it

items.d: Download the zip file, send it to the AI and say: "Install the skill in this file following the INSTALL.md inside."
When a job is done, say: "Please review how we did [job name]" (add "and hand off" if you need to open a new session).

sections.t: Frequently asked questions

items.q: Will the AI change your instructions or memory on its own?
items.a: No. The AI only gives proposals after filtering them carefully. It saves only what you approve, and anything you don't agree to stays as it is.

items.q: Does the skill dig back through your old conversations?
items.a: No. The skill only looks back at the conversation session that is currently open. It does not go through your older sessions.

items.q: Does this skill summarize meetings or documents, or write a new skill by itself?
items.a: No. The skill only looks back at the conversation you just finished. It does not summarize meetings or documents, and it does not write a brand-new skill from scratch.

items.q: What if I use a web chat app that can't write files?
items.a: The review is shown right in the chat window for you to save. For approved proposals, the AI gives you ready-made text to paste into the right place yourself.

items.q: What if the AI can't install the skill from the zip file by itself?
items.a: Unzip the file. Then, each time you want a review, attach SKILL.md, assets/journal-template.md and assets/handoff-template.md at the end of that conversation and say "Follow SKILL.md". The review will appear right in the chat window for you to save yourself.

items.q: Once this skill is installed, will the AI never repeat an old mistake again?
items.a: We don't promise that. The skill helps lessons get saved in the right place, so the AI has something to rely on next time. The AI still needs that place to write to, because it can't remember on its own. The handoff note is also only as accurate as what the AI is able to read.

How it runs, step by step

items.d: The skill checks whether the root folder already has PRODUCT.md or DESIGN.md. If you mention a website or logo, it reads the quick-start section of the reference docs to shorten the visual questions.

Interviews one cluster at a time, each question with a suggested answer and a reason. Done when every section is filled or marked N/A with a reason, there is at least one real answer from the student, and you confirm the DRAFT.
Builds design-explore.html with 3 style families to choose from by eye. Every color pair must pass contrast before you see it. After you choose, tokens are locked from the chosen version.

An independent subagent that never saw the interview checks the files against the completion criteria. Every finding must be fixed or explained.

sections.t: Phase 1: PRODUCT.md interview questions

Interviews in Vietnamese, one cluster of questions at a time, waiting for answers before the next cluster. No dumping every question at once, no trickling single isolated questions either. Each question comes with a suggested answer and a reason, because fixing a wrong guess is faster than filling a blank.

head: Cluster
Questions
rows: Product or project name (if none yet, suggest 2 to 3 working names). A one-line tagline: what it is, who it's for. 1 to 2 sentences on what the product does and what problem it solves. Register: brand (the design is the product, like a landing page, portfolio or campaign, strong expression allowed) or product (the design serves the product, like a dashboard or app, prioritizing clarity, efficiency, consistency).
Who uses it: describe a real person with a role and context, not something generic. What they need to get done when they open the product. What success looks like: one concrete sign, not 'satisfied'.

3 words for the brand's personality, avoiding 'beautiful' or 'professional' because they're too generic. 2 to 3 products or sites whose feel you want, and why each. What it must never look like (specific names). Special accessibility needs, WCAG AA by default, such as older users, large text, color blindness, reduced motion.

items: Register holds a single value, brand or product, no prose. This value also decides the sample screen set in phase 2.
Cluster 2: the skill proposes a reasonable answer based on cluster 1 as a hypothesis for the student to correct.
The must-never-look-like items (anti-references) matter a lot, because they appear word for word in the Don'ts section of DESIGN.md.
Where the wording matters, quote the student's exact words in double quotes.
No talk of colors, fonts or corner radius in this phase; that's phase 2's job.

sections.t: Deriving design principles

The skill doesn't ask directly; it derives 3 to 5 strategic principles from the answers, for example 'reading speed matters more than effects' for a product used by busy professionals. These are strategy, not visual rules (no hex codes or fonts). The skill states them for the student to confirm.
Information gate and fallback paths

items: Before writing: every section of the template is filled or marked N/A with a reason. If something is missing, go back to that cluster and ask again, never make it up. Then create PRODUCT.md in the root folder from the template, labelled [DRAFT] until the student confirms.
At least one real answer from the student is required, not synthesized from the brief.
Student only gives adjectives for personality: ask once 'if the brand were a person you met, how would they talk and dress?', then write [needs input] and move on.
No must-never-look-like items: ask once more 'what kind of design would feel wrong for this brand?'. Still nothing, write N/A and note that the Don'ts section will be derived from the principles.
File already exists: ask which file to refresh, never overwrite without asking.

sections.t: If you already have or like a website (quick start)

The skill asks whether there's a website or page you want to follow or learn from, then classifies it. If it's your own brand, keep its identity; if it's a page you admire, take only the direction, since it isn't your brand. If there's none, run the full interview.

items: For any link, send it to context.dev's design-md-generator tool (context.dev/free-tools/design-md-generator), which returns a DESIGN.md for that page. No need to save HTML or take screenshots.

That output is only reference material, not the final file. Take the hex codes, fonts, corner radius and spacing as a draft for the DESIGN.md frontmatter, note what's missing or renamed, then still go through the pick-by-eye and contrast-check steps.
If the tool or link has changed, trust the current tool and tell the student.

Asset handling

Don't copy the original logo or fonts: they're intellectual property and not your brand. Inherit only the style and structure. If you don't have a logo yet, note it in UPLOAD.md

sections.t: Inherited colors are not exempt from the contrast check either.
Phase 2 in detail: from feel to DESIGN.md
Phase 2 requires PRODUCT.md. Principle: describe the direction in words first, lock the numbers by eye later. Never ask students for hex codes, fonts or corner radius.

items.d: One cluster, each question with a suggested answer. (1) Core feeling: what a stranger should feel in the first 3 seconds, 3 words, the more specific the better. (2) Metaphor: if the brand were a room you walk into, what room is it, the light, the atmosphere, the materials. (3) Color personality: pick a level (a) neutrals plus one accent at no more than 10%, (b) one dominant color at 30 to 60%, (c) a 3 to 4 color palette, (d) color across the whole surface, then describe the range in words. (4) Type feel: (a) elegant serif plus friendly sans, (b) one clean sans, (c) strong display plus mono, (d) magazine style. (5) Motion energy: restrained, responsive, or choreographed. (6) Depth: flat, lightly layered or clearly raised; product should be flat or layered, brand is free. (7) Reconfirm the must-never-look-like items from PRODUCT.md.

Three families that truly differ in visual language (frame style, corner radius, depth, density, decoration, layout school), not recolors of one design. A stays closest to the student's words, B pushes the personality, C is light and easy to read (also a test: if C wins, A and B went too far). At least one family breaks away from the obvious choice. Based on styles.csv, colors.csv and a Vietnamese-ready font pair from typography.csv.

Fill specimen.html into design-explore.html in the root folder, one file with 3 tabs A, B, C. Each tab uses the brand's real copy (name, tagline, 2 to 3 sentences verbatim from PRODUCT.md, no lorem), a Vietnamese diacritics test line, the screen set for the Register, a primary button in 3 states and an embedded JS WCAG contrast reader.

items.t: Step 4: check contrast before the student looks
items.d: Every text and background pair must pass WCAG AA. If one fails, adjust the token (darker or lighter) within the family's personality; if it still fails, switch to the nearest palette in colors.csv that covers all roles. Repeat until everything passes. The student never sees a failing option.

Ask by feel: which one looks most like you. Students can mix (A's colors with B's type), applied directly to CSS variables and rechecked for contrast, with a reminder to press Ctrl+F5 and a log of every change. Reconfirm in plain words, for example 'soft, warm, rounded'.

items.t: Step 6: lock DESIGN.md from the chosen version
items.d: Read each CSS value from the confirmed version, never write from memory, because any value not in DESIGN.md gets lost downstream (Claude Design reads DESIGN.md, not the specimen). Every must-never-look-like item from PRODUCT.md goes into Don'ts verbatim. The Motion section carries the NON-SPEC EXTENSION mark.

head: Register
Sample screen set
rows: Hero, call-to-action button (3 states), proof card, short form
App shell (top or side navigation), data table row, card, form, button (3 states)

items: Student can't choose or feels they're all wrong: ask in words what's wrong, adjust the closest family and show it again, never invent a fourth family.
Chosen font fails the Vietnamese filter: replace it using vn-fonts.md, keeping the personality.
Design mode without PRODUCT.md: stop and run phase 1 first, because the Register and the must-never-look-like items are required inputs.

Mapping Vietnamese words to search keywords in the data: sang trọng is luxury or elegant, ấm áp is warm or humanist, gọn hiện đại is minimal or modern, mạnh gắt is bold or brutalist, vui is playful or rounded.

sections.t: DESIGN.md format (Stitch standard, 9 sections)

The source standard is the open-source Stitch spec (google-labs-code/design.md, 8 sections plus a version field). The skill adds a single extension, Motion, clearly marked as non-standard. The frontmatter is mandatory and machine-read; the body is the rationale for human readers and never redefines token values in prose that contradicts the frontmatter.

---
version: alpha
name: Project name
description: One-line tagline
colors:
  primary: "#1A1C1E"
  secondary: "#6C7278"
  accent: "#B8422E"
  background: "#FFFFFF"
  foreground: "#1A1C1E"
typography:
  h1:
    fontFamily: "Public Sans"
    fontSize: "48px"
    fontWeight: 600
    lineHeight: 1.1
    letterSpacing: "-0.02em"
rounded:
  sm: "4px"
  md: "8px"
  lg: "16px"
spacing:
  xs: "4px"
  sm: "8px"
  md: "16px"
  lg: "32px"
components:
  button-primary:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.primary}"
    textColor: "#FFFFFF"
    rounded: "{rounded.sm}"
    padding: "12px 24px"
---

items: version is required. Colors are written as sRGB hex (#RGB, #RGBA, #RRGGBB, #RRGGBBAA). Token references use the {path.to.token} form.

Color role names are lowercase for core roles (primary, secondary, accent, background, foreground, card, muted, border, ring, destructive); text-on-background colors use onX (onPrimary) or xForeground (mutedForeground). Stay consistent within a file.
Component sub-tokens are limited to: backgroundColor, textColor, typography, rounded, padding, size, height, width.
Fonts must include the Vietnamese character set.

head: Section (exact name, exact order)
Content
rows: A north star (one metaphor) and 2 to 3 sentences on personality, density and aesthetic philosophy, ending with Key Characteristics. Includes the Register and the must-never-look-like items from PRODUCT.md
One sentence describing the palette, then each role: color name (#HEX), where it's used and why. Named Rules optional
Display and Body fonts (with fallbacks), 1 to 2 sentences on the pair's personality, then the hierarchy: level (weight, size, line height) and purpose
Grid, columns, container width, density, breakpoints, spacing rhythm on the spacing scale
Shadows or tonal layering; if flat, say so explicitly
Corner language (per rounded), border style, geometric motifs (pill, sharp, organic)
Extension section, marked NON-SPEC EXTENSION. Motion energy and which interactions animate. Short
Buttons, cards or containers, inputs. Only components that actually exist
Do: specific instructions with exact values. Don't: specific bans, with every must-never-look-like item from PRODUCT.md appearing verbatim

items: Decisive voice: 'never', 'always', 'forbidden', no 'consider' or 'may'.
Describe by feel rather than jargon: 'gently rounded corners (8px)' beats 'rounded-lg'.
No sections beyond the 9, no renaming, no made-up components.

sections.t: Vietnamese-ready fonts

items: Hard filter: a font can only be used if it has the vietnamese subset, because diacritics like ậ ằ ễ ợ ữ break in fonts without it. Check the Subsets column in google-fonts.csv (505 fonts pass, per the skill docs).
Safe default pair: Be Vietnam Pro (headings) and Noto Sans (body). Use it when unsure or when the chosen font fails the filter.
Replacement: if a font lacks the Vietnamese subset, switch to the closest font of the same kind (serif for serif, mono for mono) or fall back to the default pair. Never use a font without Vietnamese.
The specimen loads fonts via a Google Fonts link tag (students are online); 'one file' means one HTML file, not offline use.

rows: Turn on Developer mode in Settings, go to Plugins/Apps > Browse > + > custom app, paste the URL and create.

sections.t: Menu names and plan permissions on each platform change often; if your screen doesn't match, check the compatibility table in the app's guide.
Use it properly and safely
The app lets web AI read and possibly edit files in folders you grant access to. Always start with read-only access, don't add a whole drive, and never share your connection link.

items: Permissions per workspace: read, edit files, create/delete/rename, run tasks, write to local Git. Start read-only and only turn on writing when needed.
The app blocks sensitive areas like .env files, SSH folders, private keys and credentials, and skips build/cache folders. Even so, don't put secrets in a workspace.
Don't add a whole drive: it's slow and pulls in unrelated files. Keep source code folders separate from output folders.
Turning on Git write doesn't mean it pushes automatically. SSH commands are risky and need a separate permission.
Don't edit or share the connection link: anyone with it can access your workspace.
Stick to UTF-8 text and code files; PDF, DOCX and XLSX aren't read reliably yet, so convert them to text first.
Tell the AI to diagnose first, and only edit or run commands after you agree.

items.q: Which computers does it run on?

items.q: Will the AI edit files or push code on its own?
items.a: The AI can only do what you allow in each workspace: read, edit files, create/delete/rename, run tasks, write to local Git. Turning on Git write doesn't mean it pushes automatically, and SSH commands need a separate permission. Start read-only and tell the AI to diagnose first, editing only after you agree.

items.q: Are secret files like .env sent to the AI?
items.a: The app blocks sensitive areas like .env files, SSH folders, private keys and credentials. Even so, don't put secrets in a workspace, and never share the connection link, since anyone with it can access your workspace.

items.q: Can it read PDF, Word or Excel files?
items.a: Not reliably yet. Stick to UTF-8 text and code files; convert PDF, DOCX and XLSX to text first.

items.q: Is the app open source, and how is data stored?
items.a: The site doesn't say whether the app is open source, its license, privacy policy details (there's a separate Privacy page), or how data is stored and encrypted. Read the terms and privacy policy before using it on important projects.

sections.t: What it is

Zalo Switcher (MIT license, README in Vietnamese) lets you keep several Zalo accounts on the same computer and open them at the same time, each with its own data folder and its own Zalo window. Good for people managing several accounts (personal, work, fanpage…) who don't want to keep logging out.
Quick install

items.d: Download Zalo-Switcher-…-macOS.zip from Releases and drag it into Applications. Since the app isn't notarized by Apple, the first time you need to allow it in System Settings > Privacy & Security (Open Anyway).

Run ZaloSwitcher-Setup-<version>.exe (no admin rights needed) or unzip and run ZaloSwitcher.exe. SmartScreen may warn you because the file isn't signed: choose More info > Run anyway if you trust the source.
Save the Zalo account you're logged into as the main Zalo (if you aren't logged in, the first account you add becomes the main one).
Click Add account, name it, log into Zalo in the new window, then use Open on each account.

sections.t: Limits to know

items: Zalo still allows only one session per type (phone, desktop, web) per account; this tool doesn't change that rule.
Only open accounts receive messages and notifications.
Voice and video calls only work reliably in one window at a time.
Each window uses as much RAM as a separate Zalo, and each account takes a few GB of disk space.
It depends on how Zalo stores data, so a Zalo update can break the tool: read the README before updating Zalo.

sections.t: FAQ

items.q: Does opening several accounts change Zalo's session rules?
items.a: No. Zalo still allows only one session per type (phone, desktop, web) per account.

items.q: Will it still work after I update Zalo?
items.a: Not guaranteed. The tool depends on how Zalo stores data, so a Zalo update can break it. Read the README before updating Zalo.

items.q: Is the project stable?
items.a: It's new: about 18 stars, a few dozen commits, tested on 20-21/10/2026 per the README, version 1.2.0. Read the README carefully and download files only from the repo's own Releases page.

items.t: You want your own account to reply automatically
items.before: Opening Zalo to read and answer every message yourself.
items.after: A bot listens through the listener, processes the content and calls the send function. The README has an echo bot example you can try.

items.before: Reminders live in another app you rarely open.
items.after: Your program sends reminders into Zalo, where you already read every day.

items.t: Your system needs to send alerts
items.before: System notifications sit somewhere else and nobody sees them in time.
items.after: Forward system notifications into Zalo with the send function.

sections.t: See it in action: input → process → output
An echo bot on your own spare Zalo account

input.label: Your code (bot.js)

steps: You run node bot.js and the library shows a QR code to log in.
You scan the QR with Zalo on the spare account's phone.
The listener receives personal and group messages sent to the account.
The bot processes the text and calls the send function to reply.

output.label: Terminal and Zalo chat
output.t:
$ node bot.js
QR code created, scan it with Zalo on your phone
Logged in: spare account "Test Bot"
Listener started, waiting for messages...
[incoming] Friend A: What time is the meeting tomorrow?
[sent] Echo: What time is the meeting tomorrow?

--- In Friend A's Zalo ---
Friend A:  What time is the meeting tomorrow?
Test Bot:  Echo: What time is the meeting tomorrow?

sections.note: Illustrative example, real content depends on your code. Unofficial library: test only on a spare account, needs Node.js or Bun.

sections.t: What it is

zca-js is a JavaScript/TypeScript library (installed via npm or Bun, MIT license) that lets your program log into a personal Zalo account, then listen for and send messages, just like using Zalo Web. Good for personal bots, automated notifications or plugging Zalo into your workflows.
Quick start

items.d: In a Node.js project run: npm install zca-js (or bun add zca-js).
Create new Zalo() then call loginQR(), and scan the QR code with Zalo on your phone.
Use api.listener.on("message", …) to receive messages, then api.listener.start().
Process the content and call the send function. The README has an echo bot example you can try.

sections.t: Use it for the right things

items: Good for: auto-reply bots for your own account, reminders, forwarding system notifications into Zalo, learning and experimenting.
Not for: spam, mass messaging strangers, collecting other people's data. It breaks Zalo's terms and easily gets your account locked.
Each account can only run one web listener at a time; opening Zalo Web in a browser will stop the listener.
The project is under heavy development (hundreds of commits, many open issues): usage may change between versions, so read the latest README.

sections.t: FAQ

items.q: Can my account get locked?
items.a: It can. The project emulates a browser to talk to Zalo Web, and the README warns that accounts can be locked or banned and the author takes no responsibility. Only test on a secondary account.

items.q: Can I use it for mass messaging?
items.a: You shouldn't. Spam, mass messaging strangers or collecting other people's data breaks Zalo's terms and easily gets your account locked.

items.q: Why does the listener stop by itself?
items.a: Each account can only run one web listener at a time. Opening Zalo Web in a browser will stop the listener.

items.q: What if old sample code stops working?
items.a: The project is under heavy development (hundreds of commits, many open issues), so usage may change between versions; for example, sending images since v2 needs a metadata function. Read the latest README.

items.q: How big is the project?
items.a: As of 24/10/2026: about 688 stars, MIT license.

sections.t: Test on a secondary account and read the latest README before building a bot

tool-phone-laptop-devmode.title: Connect your phone to a laptop with Developer Mode (Android + iOS)
tool-phone-laptop-devmode.note: Turn on Developer options, install adb, connect by cable and wirelessly, control the screen with scrcpy; iPhone: Developer Mode, Xcode, Safari Web Inspector, libimobiledevice. All commands included.

sections.t: Your phone stays in your pocket, the work happens on your laptop
sections.lead: Copy photos, record a screen demo, run commands and debug web pages on your phone without picking it up. Turn on Developer Mode once, plug in a cable or connect over Wi-Fi, and do the rest from your laptop keyboard.
ticks: Android: almost everything through adb
View and control the screen with scrcpy
iPhone: logs, screen mirroring, Safari web debugging

sections.t: What your laptop can do with your phone

items.d: Install and uninstall apps, copy files both ways, take screenshots and record the screen, read logs, type and tap remotely. adb comes free with Google's SDK Platform-Tools.
Turn on Wireless debugging, pair once per laptop with a 6-digit code, then adb connect over Wi-Fi. Android 10 and earlier use adb tcpip 5555.
Open source, no app on the phone, runs on the same adb connection. Tap with your laptop's mouse and keyboard, and record while you watch.
No adb and no remote control. You can view logs, record and mirror the screen, debug web pages with Safari Web Inspector, and install dev apps with Xcode on a Mac.

sections.t: Everyday jobs get lighter with your phone connected

sections.t: See it in action: input → process → output
Pulling a whole photo folder from an Android phone to the laptop with one command

input.label: Command
input.t:
adb devices -l
adb pull /sdcard/DCIM/Camera/ ./anh

steps: You turn on USB debugging on the phone and plug in a data cable.
You tap Allow USB debugging on the phone.
adb devices -l confirms the phone shows as device.
adb pull copies the whole photo folder to the laptop.

output.label: Terminal
output.t:
$ adb devices -l
List of devices attached
R58N123ABC   device usb:1-1 product:a54x model:SM_A546E device:a54x

$ adb pull /sdcard/DCIM/Camera/ ./anh
/sdcard/DCIM/Camera/: 312 files pulled, 0 skipped. 18.4 MB/s (1873451520 bytes in 97.1s)

$ ls ./anh/Camera | head -3
20261102_081530.jpg
20261102_081602.jpg
20261103_174411.mp4

sections.note: Illustrative example, file count and device name depend on your phone. Needs adb (SDK Platform-Tools); turn USB debugging off when done.

sections.t: Android can do almost everything through adb (install apps, copy files, view the screen, run commands). Apple locks the iPhone down much more: mostly logs, screen recording/mirroring and web debugging. This guide covers each system separately.
Only turn on Developer Mode / USB debugging on your own phone and only trust your own laptop. This permission gives the laptop deep control over the phone; don't use public computers.
PART 1 · ANDROID
Step 1: Turn on Developer options

items.d: Samsung: About phone → Software information. Some phones: Settings → About phone.
The phone shows “You are now a developer”. Enter your PIN/password if asked.
Usually under Settings → System → Developer options (Samsung: at the bottom of the main Settings page).
Xiaomi/Redmi: also turn on “Install via USB” and “USB debugging (Security settings)” if you want to control it with a mouse.

sections.t: Step 2: Install adb on the laptop
adb comes with Google's SDK Platform-Tools, free.

# Windows: download the zip at developer.android.com/tools/releases/platform-tools, unzip it,
# open PowerShell in that folder and type  .\adb version

# macOS
brew install --cask android-platform-tools

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install adb

# Check
adb version
Step 3: Plug in the cable and allow access

items.t: Use a USB cable that transfers data
items.d: A charge-only cable won't be detected. If the phone asks for a USB mode, choose “File transfer”.

items.t: Tap “Allow USB debugging” on the phone
items.d: Tick “Always allow from this computer” and tap Allow.
Type adb devices. A status of device means it worked.

sections.t: adb devices -l

items: unauthorized: you haven't tapped Allow on the phone. Unplug and replug the cable, or run adb kill-server then adb devices.
Device not found: try another cable/port and check that USB debugging is on. Windows may need the manufacturer's USB driver (Samsung, Xiaomi…).
Linux says “no permissions”: set up a udev rule for your phone brand, or rerun adb with the right permissions.

sections.t: Step 4: Common adb commands

# Install / uninstall apps
adb install app.apk
adb install -r app.apk          # reinstall, keep data
adb uninstall com.ten.goi

# Copy files
adb push file.txt /sdcard/Download/
adb pull /sdcard/DCIM/Camera/ ./anh

# Take a screenshot
adb shell screencap -p /sdcard/s.png
adb pull /sdcard/s.png

# Record the screen (max 3 minutes by default, Ctrl+C to stop)
adb shell screenrecord /sdcard/demo.mp4
adb pull /sdcard/demo.mp4

# Open a shell on the phone / view logs
adb shell
adb logcat

# List installed apps
adb shell pm list packages

# Type and tap remotely
adb shell input text hello
adb shell input tap 540 1200
adb shell input keyevent 4      # 4=Back, 3=Home, 26=Power

# Reboot
adb reboot

# When adb hangs
adb kill-server
adb start-server
Step 5: Connect wirelessly (Android 11 and later)
The phone and laptop must be on the same Wi-Fi network. You only need to pair once per laptop.

items.d: Developer options → Wireless debugging → on.
Tap “Pair device with pairing code”. The phone shows a pairing IP:port and a 6-digit code.

items.t: Run the pair command on the laptop
items.d: Type adb pair IP:PAIRING-PORT and enter the 6-digit code.
The main Wireless debugging screen shows a different IP:port (the connection port). Type adb connect IP:CONNECT-PORT. This port may change each time you turn it back on.

sections.t:
adb pair 192.168.1.20:37099
# enter the 6-digit code when asked
adb connect 192.168.1.20:41555
adb devices

# Disconnect
adb disconnect
sections.cap: Example (replace with the IP and ports on your phone)

sections.t: Android 10 and earlier: plug in the cable once, type adb tcpip 5555, unplug, then adb connect phone-IP:5555.
Step 6: View and control the phone screen on the laptop (scrcpy)
scrcpy is an open-source tool. It needs no app on the phone and uses the same adb connection above (cable or wireless). You can control the phone with your mouse and keyboard.

# Windows (if you have winget) or download the zip from the GitHub page (adb included)
winget install --exact Genymobile.scrcpy

# macOS
brew install scrcpy

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install scrcpy

# Run (phone has USB debugging on and is connected)
scrcpy

# Common options
scrcpy --turn-screen-off --stay-awake     # turn off the phone screen, keep it awake
scrcpy --max-size 1024                    # lower the resolution for smoother playback
scrcpy --record demo.mp4                  # watch and record at the same time
scrcpy -s SERIAL                          # pick a device when several are connected
Install commands and option names may differ depending on your scrcpy version and OS. Check the scrcpy README on GitHub for the latest commands.
Turn it off when not in use

items: Turn off USB debugging and Wireless debugging when you're done.
Developer options → “Revoke USB debugging authorizations” to remove trusted laptops.

sections.t: PART 2 · iPHONE (iOS)

Know this first: iPhone has no adb. Apple doesn't let a laptop control the screen remotely like Android. What you can do: view logs, record/mirror the screen, debug web pages in Safari, install dev apps with Xcode (Mac).
Step 1: Trust the computer

items.t: Plug the iPhone into the laptop with a cable
items.d: Use a Lightning/USB-C cable that transfers data.
Enter your passcode when asked. On Windows, also install the Apple Devices app (or iTunes) for the driver, otherwise the phone won't be detected.

sections.t: Step 2: Turn on Developer Mode (iOS 16 and later)

items.d: Scroll to the bottom and find “Developer Mode”.
The iPhone will ask to restart.
Unlock the phone, tap “Turn On” and enter your passcode.

sections.t: The Developer Mode option may not appear until the iPhone has been connected to Xcode on a Mac or has a dev build of an app installed. This is how iOS works, not a problem with your phone.
Step 3A: If you have a Mac

items.d: Open Xcode → Window → Devices and Simulators. Tick “Connect via network” to connect wirelessly after pairing by cable.
Open QuickTime Player → File → New Movie Recording, click the arrow next to the record button and choose the iPhone as the source.

iPhone: Settings → Safari → Advanced → turn on Web Inspector (on newer iOS it may be under Settings → Apps → Safari). Mac: Safari → Settings → Advanced → turn on “Show features for web developers”. Open the page on the iPhone, then go to the Develop menu on the Mac and choose the iPhone's name and the page to inspect.

sections.t: Step 3B: If you use Windows or Linux
The open-source libimobiledevice toolkit can read device info and logs. Some commands (like screenshots) depend on the iOS version: iOS 17 and later need a different tool, e.g. pymobiledevice3.

# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install libimobiledevice

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install libimobiledevice-utils usbmuxd

# Pair and check
idevicepair pair
idevice_id -l                 # list UDIDs
ideviceinfo                   # device info
idevicesyslog                 # live logs
idevicescreenshot shot.png    # may not work on iOS 17+

# iOS 17+: pymobiledevice3 (requires Python)
pip install pymobiledevice3
pymobiledevice3 usbmux list
pymobiledevice3 syslog live
Some pymobiledevice3 commands on iOS 17+ need a “tunnel” running and admin rights. See the project's docs on GitHub for the syntax for your version.
Mirror the iPhone screen to a laptop without a cable

items: Mac: use Control Center on the iPhone → Screen Mirroring, or QuickTime with a cable as above.
Windows: Windows can't receive AirPlay out of the box. You need a third-party AirPlay receiver app. Check its reliability and price yourself before using it.
This guide hasn't tested each third-party app individually.

sections.t: Security notes for both systems

items: Turn off Developer Mode (iPhone) or USB debugging (Android) when not in use.
Don't plug into public charging stations while debugging is on. If a “Trust / Allow” dialog pops up unexpectedly, tap Don't Trust / Deny.
Don't run unfamiliar adb or pip commands copied from unknown sources. Many commands can delete data.

sections.t: Sources checked

items.t: Expo: enable Developer Mode on iOS

sections.t: FAQ

items.q: Is it safe to turn on Developer Mode?
items.a: This permission gives the laptop deep control over the phone. Only turn it on for your own phone, only trust your own laptop, don't use public computers, and turn it off when you're done.

items.q: Can I control an iPhone from the laptop like an Android?
items.a: No. iPhone has no adb, and Apple doesn't let a laptop control the screen remotely. You can view logs, record and mirror the screen, debug in Safari, and install dev apps with Xcode.

items.q: adb devices says unauthorized or shows nothing. What now?
items.a: unauthorized means you haven't tapped Allow on the phone: replug the cable or run adb kill-server then adb devices. Nothing shown: use a data cable, try another port, check USB debugging is on; Windows may need the manufacturer's driver.

items.q: I can't find Developer Mode on my iPhone.
items.a: It may only appear after the iPhone has been connected to Xcode on a Mac or has a dev build of an app installed. That's how iOS works, not a problem with your phone.

items.q: Can I mirror an iPhone to Windows wirelessly?
items.a: Windows can't receive AirPlay out of the box, so you need a third-party app. Check its reliability and price yourself; this guide hasn't tested each app.

items.q: The scrcpy or pymobiledevice3 commands differ on my machine?
items.a: Command and option names may differ by version and OS. Check the scrcpy README and the pymobiledevice3 docs on GitHub for the latest syntax.

sections.t: Set it up once, work with your phone from the keyboard
sections.d: Android: turn on USB debugging, install adb, plug in and run scrcpy. iPhone: tap Trust, turn on Developer Mode, then use Xcode, Safari or libimobiledevice.
sections.note: Turn off USB debugging or Developer Mode when not in use. Don't plug into public charging stations while debugging is on, and don't run unfamiliar adb or pip commands: many can delete data.

MCP is an open standard for connecting agents to tools and data, like a USB port for AI. Agent Skills package instructions plus scripts so an agent can redo a task the right way.

sections.t: Personal agents that run on your own machine or server

items.d: A personal agent running in the background on your machine, taking commands via WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack…; it can run commands, manage files, control a browser and automate tasks. Former names: Clawdbot, Moltbot; author Peter Steinberger. Note: its permissions are very broad, so run it in an isolated environment and grant access carefully.

A self-hosted agent that runs as a background process: persistent memory, writes its own skills from repeated tasks, many chat gateways (Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp…), scheduled runs, any model you like. Launched around February 2026. You still pay for the model and the server.

sections.t: Coding agents

items.d: An agent that reads and edits code and runs commands in your project folder; supports skills, hooks, MCP and subagents. Also available in IDEs and as a desktop app.
OpenAI's coding agent: runs as a CLI, in an IDE, or hands tasks to a cloud version to work on several in parallel so you can review the results.

A coding environment Google launched in late 2025 with the agent at its center: the agent plans, writes code, runs a browser to test, and leaves “artifacts” (plans, screenshots, recordings) for you to review. Uses Gemini and some other models.

A code editor built on VS Code with deep AI integration: chat, multi-file edits, an Agent mode that runs commands and fixes errors itself, plus background agents in the cloud. Lets you choose from many models.

Started as code suggestions, now has Agent mode in VS Code and a coding agent that takes GitHub issues, creates a branch, writes code and opens a pull request for you to review. Best fit if your team already uses GitHub.
Google's open-source command-line agent, in the same group as Claude Code and Codex CLI.
An IDE with an agent (Cascade) that understands the whole project, competing directly with Cursor.
An autonomous agent you assign work to like an engineer: it picks up tasks, writes code, tests it and sends back results.

sections.t: Standards and building blocks

items.d: An open standard for connecting agents to tools and data, like a “USB port” for AI. Anthropic announced it in late 2024, and many companies now support it.
A bundle of instructions plus scripts so an agent can redo a task the right way. It's an open standard, just donated to the Agentic AI Foundation (news from 22/10/2026 in AI News).

sections.t: General-purpose agents (no coding needed)

items.d: Turn on tools, browse the web, run code and read files right in the app you already use for multi-step work. The easiest place to start.
A cloud agent that takes a goal, then researches, writes reports, builds web pages and sends back the results on its own.

items.d: Connect apps with drag-and-drop workflows and add AI steps. Good for “fixed workflow” level tasks, easy to control, beginner-friendly.

Organize several role-based agents to work together.
Microsoft's framework for agents to talk to and coordinate with each other.

sections.t: What the tool does for you

items.t: Read Facebook without opening a browser
items.d: fb feed, posts, view, profile, friends, search, notifs show you the feed, posts, comments, profiles, friends and notifications. Chrome runs headless: no window, no stolen focus.

sections.t: Important notes before use

items: Facebook's terms restrict automated access. Only use it on your own account, at a human-like pace, and accept the risk of account restrictions. This is the repo README's own assessment.
Login cookies live in the ~/.cache/fb profile (or %LOCALAPPDATA%\fb on Windows). Anyone who can read this folder can use your session, so treat it like a password.
The headless Chrome is controlled via the DevTools protocol on a random 127.0.0.1 port with no authentication. Only use it on a personal machine, not a shared one.
Post, comment, send and delete commands are real actions on your account. With an AI agent, try read-only mode first and require confirmation before posting or sending.
Facebook's interface can change at any time, so the tool may need updates. The repo states clearly that not every feature is guaranteed to be tested.
End-to-end encrypted chats need your Messenger PIN: pass it via the FB_PIN variable or stdin, not as a command argument.

items.a: Cookies live in ~/.cache/fb (or %LOCALAPPDATA%\fb on Windows), and anyone who can read that folder can use your session. The headless Chrome takes commands on a random 127.0.0.1 port with no authentication, so only use it on a personal machine.

items.q: Should I let an AI agent post and send messages on its own?
items.a: Post, comment, send and delete are real actions on your account. Run the agent read-only first and require confirmation before posting or sending.

sections.lead: This card gathers the filming basics: choosing shot sizes and angles, composing the frame, setting up the light and preparing your gear. At the end there is a five-step checklist before you hit record.

sections.t: What you'll learn

sections.t: Sources: university video production guides and roundup articles on the web (see the end of this card). One is a 2008 checklist, so I only took the principles, not the old gear names. Most Vietnamese articles I found only covered gimbals and mics, so the angles and lighting parts come from English sources.
1. Shot sizes and camera angles
Cover all the shot sizes: wide shots for information, close shots for emotion. Also shoot B-roll and cutaways so you have something to insert when editing, especially for interviews.
2. Composition: the rule of thirds

Split the frame with 2 horizontal and 2 vertical lines and place the subject on a line or intersection. It's a guideline, not a hard rule, so break it when the shot needs it. Many cameras have a built-in grid to make this easy.
3. Lighting: 3-point lighting and reflectors

head: Light
Where to place it
What it does
rows: About 45 degrees in front of the subject
Opposite the key, about half its intensity
Separates the subject from the background

items: No fill light yet? Use a reflector or a white card instead, per the checklist.
Avoid strong light right behind the subject, as it easily turns them dark or into a silhouette.
Set white balance to match the light source, such as daylight or tungsten.

rows: Use one whenever you can; handheld is harder to keep steady than it feels

Check audio levels before shooting. A directional mic picks up sound in front clearly and cuts surrounding noise. Use a windscreen outdoors
Stabilizes with motors and sensors, helps with tricky shots like POV and 360-degree rotation. Check phone compatibility and decide what you'll shoot before buying
Charged batteries, script or shot list

sections.t: What it is

Social AIO (formerly FB AIO, Tools category on the Chrome Web Store, version 2.1, updated 31/7/2026) is a toolbox that bundles many social media management tasks into one extension. Per the store page, it has about 30,000 users and a 5.0 rating from about 2.8 thousand reviews. The developer states it isn't affiliated with any social media platform.
How to use

items.d: Open the extension page on the Chrome Web Store, click Add to Chrome and read the requested permissions.

items.t: Log in to social media as usual
items.d: The extension works on the pages you have open, so log in to the account you want to manage first.
Try a task on a few items (one post, a few people) to see the result before doing it in bulk.
The store page links to the developer's support site (fbaio.org) and GitHub issues.

sections.t: Use it for the right things

items: Good for: backing up your own content, cleaning up a personal account, more privacy, tracking how much time you spend.
Be careful: bulk actions on accounts used for work, ads or fanpages. Going too fast can trigger the platform's anti-bot checks.
Don't use it to download or repost other people's content without permission.
The extension can read the social media pages you open: only install from the official store, keep an eye on updates and remove it if you no longer use it.

sections.t: FAQ

items.q: Can this extension affect my account?
items.a: It can. Bulk actions such as deleting posts, unfriending and unfollowing are hard to undo and may break platform terms. Going too fast can trigger the platform's anti-bot checks. Try on a few items first.

items.q: Should I use it on a fanpage or an ads account?
items.a: Be careful. Accounts used for work, ads or fanpages are where you should avoid fast bulk actions.

items.q: Can I download other people's content?
items.a: Not without permission. The extension is meant for backing up your own content, not for downloading or reposting other people's.

items.q: What can the extension read?
items.a: It can read the social media pages you open. Only install from the official store, review the permissions when installing, keep an eye on updates and remove it if you no longer use it. The description and privacy commitments are the developer's own words on the store page, not independently verified.

items.q: Where do I get help?
items.a: The store page links to the developer's support site (fbaio.org) and GitHub issues.
